questions.prompt: What structure gives a plant cell its rigid, boxy shape and helps it resist bursting?
questions.explanation: The cell wall is a tough layer made of cellulose fibers that surrounds the cell membrane, giving the cell a fixed shape and letting it resist the internal pressure of water without bursting.
questions.misconception: Many learners think the cell membrane — which every cell, plant or animal, has — is the rigid part. But the cell membrane is thin and flexible; it's the cell wall, found only in plant cells (not animal cells), that provides the rigid, boxy shape.

questions.prompt: Why do plant cells contain chloroplasts while animal cells do not?
options: Chloroplasts capture sunlight to make food through photosynthesis, which plants need because they can't eat food the way animals do
Chloroplasts store water for the cell
Chloroplasts break down the cell's waste materials
Chloroplasts help the cell divide into two cells
questions.explanation: Plants can't move around to find food, so they make their own using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide in a process called photosynthesis, which happens inside chloroplasts. Animals get energy by eating food instead, so their cells never evolved chloroplasts.
questions.misconception: Some learners mix up chloroplasts with mitochondria because both deal with energy. But chloroplasts capture light energy and build food (photosynthesis), while mitochondria — present in both plant and animal cells — release energy from that food (cellular respiration).

questions.prompt: What is the main job of the large central vacuole in a plant cell?
options: It stores water and other materials, and its water pressure pushes against the cell wall to help keep the plant firm and upright
questions.explanation: The central vacuole fills with water, creating internal pressure (turgor pressure) that pushes outward against the cell wall, similar to how air pressure keeps a balloon firm. This is a big reason a plant wilts when it doesn't get enough water — the vacuoles lose pressure.
questions.misconception: A common mistake is treating the vacuole as empty, inactive space, or confusing it with the nucleus. It's actually an active storage and pressure-support structure — the part that holds the cell's DNA and gives instructions is the nucleus, not the vacuole.

questions.prompt: If you compared a plant cell and an animal cell side by side, which set of structures would appear ONLY in the plant cell?
options: Cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole
questions.explanation: Nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, cell membrane, cytoplasm, Golgi apparatus, and endoplasmic reticulum all appear in both plant and animal cells. What sets a plant cell apart is its cell wall, its chloroplasts, and typically one large central vacuole (animal cells may have small vacuoles, but not one dominant one).
questions.misconception: Learners often assume mitochondria are plant-only because they're taught right alongside chloroplasts in the same lesson. In fact, mitochondria appear in almost all eukaryotic cells, plant and animal alike — it's specifically the wall, the chloroplasts, and the big central vacuole that make plant cells distinct.
